title: Loom body-control protocol
description: The single source of truth for the control messages exchanged with a Loom player-body process (the Node/Mineflayer body in body/). A controller sends a BodyRequest; the process answers with exactly one BodyResponse or one BodyError, on the same line-delimited loopback socket. This is deliberately NOT the perception/decision contract in loom.schema.json: that one carries what an agent knows and decides, while this one carries lifecycle, bounded raw sense, and explicit one-shot operations against request-scoped offers. Nothing here chooses a target, item, tool, recipe, weapon, bed, role, threshold, or follow-on goal. Dig, collect, place, equip, craft, attack, sleep, eat, move, and flee each act only on authority a controller named from one retained sense answer; mutable state is re-read immediately before use; conflicting work is refused rather than multiplexed; and halt or shutdown bounds cleanup. Union types use internal tagging: BodyRequest.op and BodyResponse.op select the variant and the variant's fields are inlined alongside it. JSON Schema sees a parsed number rather than the literal that carried it, so validation keywords cannot express this wire's numeric work guard: both codecs refuse a numeric literal longer than 32 characters, or one whose decimal-point shift would make exact integrality or range checking unbounded. Those are contract rules stated in prose here and enforced before either codec materialises such a value.

ProtocolVersion.description: The protocol generation the frame is written in. Present on every frame in both directions, and checked before any generation-specific field is interpreted. Generation 6 is current. It moved from 5 because a dig report may now answer blockGone after the dig was handed to Mineflayer, when another player broke the block first; generation 5 moved from 4 because the body-chosen entity, block, and dropped-item response lists widened from 24 to 48 entries. Widening a body-chosen answer can hand an older controller a frame it never agreed to read. The const is a numeric value rather than a spelling, so 6, 6.0 and 6e0 all name this generation.

ControlId.description: A bounded identifier: a requestId correlating one request with its one answer, or the agentId naming whose body the process is. Length-bounded because it is echoed back into a frame and into logs, and character-bounded to the set below because an id is a handle rather than free text - a newline would break the framing, and a path separator or whitespace is how a local path or a free-text transport error would arrive in something that gets logged.

Username.description: The Minecraft account name the body process logs in under, bounded by Minecraft's own rule rather than by one of Loom's, because a name outside it cannot log in at all. Offline mode derives a uuid from this name, so it is also what makes an agent's identity stable across runs - and what makes a dead identity come back dead.

StatusCount.description: A millisecond duration or a tally, as a status report carries it. The upper bound is JavaScript's largest exactly-representable integer, not the widest integer either binding could hold: left unbounded above, this schema admitted a number the JVM binding encodes happily and the Node binding cannot read back, so a frame was valid to the contract and to one runtime and invalid to the other - and there was then no largest legal frame for either codec's frame-size bound to be measured against. Bounded to what the narrower runtime can represent is the only version of the bound both sides can hold. Each binding states the same number for itself, because nothing on this wire is schema-validated at runtime. The type is a number's value and not its spelling, as with ProtocolVersion above: 1000 and 1e3 are the same count, while 5.5 is no count at all however it is written.

ResourceName.description: The name the game's own data gives a thing - an entity kind, a block, an item - reported exactly as the client library read it and never translated. Lowercase because a Minecraft resource location is lowercase by the game's own rule, so a name outside this set is not a name the registry could have held. Character-bounded for the reason ControlId is: a name is echoed into a frame and into logs, and a free-text error, a host name or a local path must not be able to arrive through a field that looks like a registry name. The shape is an optional namespace followed by a path of one or more non-empty segments, rather than a flat class of the same characters, and that structure is what makes the last sentence true rather than nearly true: a flat class admitted /tmp/secret, which is lowercase throughout and so passed every other guard either codec has. A resource location never begins or ends with a slash and never doubles one, so requiring non-empty segments refuses every absolute path while still admitting the nested paths a modded registry can hold. A relative lowercase token such as tmp/secret is still admitted, and honestly so: it is indistinguishable from a legal nested id, exactly as a dotted host name is indistinguishable from a legal ControlId. That extends to a traversal - ../../etc/passwd is admitted, because a dot is a legal resource-location character and .. is therefore a legal path segment, so refusing it would make this field stricter than the registry it mirrors. It is safe here and would not be on ControlId: an agent id names Loom's own ledger and log files, while nothing anywhere reads this field as a path - it is looked up in a registry, shown to an operator, and given to a mind as a word. Length-bounded at 40 because the longest name vanilla ships is 35 characters, and because the largest legal frame has to stay computable: a name is one byte per character here, so the worst case a frame-size bound is measured against is arithmetic rather than a guess.

WorldPosition.description: A position in the world the body is standing in, as three numbers in x, y, z order. Absolute rather than relative to the body, and unmeasured: no distance, bearing or height difference is computed here, because those are what the coordinator derives and its own perception contract already has a vocabulary for. Every position in one answer is read in the same instant, which is what lets a distance derived from two of them be one reading rather than two that can disagree while the world moves. Bounded by the world border's own limit, which also keeps each number's literal short enough for the frame's numeric work guard and for the largest-legal-frame arithmetic. Note that the two runtimes spell an integral real number differently by default - Node writes 20 where the JVM writes 20.0 - and neither is made to imitate the other, because a codec that reshaped a number it had read correctly would be editing evidence to make a test pass. Nothing is lost by that: each direction of this wire has exactly one encoder in production, since a request is written by the controller and an answer by the body, so the difference can only ever reach the shared fixtures, which are re-encoded on both sides. A fixture carrying a real number therefore keeps to a value both runtimes spell identically - a non-integral one such as 12.5 - in the same spirit as the perception contract's fixtures keeping away from values that need exponential notation.

SenseRadius.description: How far from the body a sense request looks, in blocks, as the caller states it. It is on the request and not a constant of the body process, so the radius stays one number owned by the coordinator whose perception policy it is: a body holding its own copy would be a second policy able to drift from the one the perception contract's bound is stated in. The maximum is the widest a caller may ask for rather than what any caller does ask for, and is deliberately above Loom's own perception radius so that raising that radius does not need this contract to move.

SenseLimit.description: How many entries each bounded world-observation list may carry, as the caller states it. The same limit is independently applied to entities, nearby blocks, and dropped items, and each list carries its own omission count. Craftable recipes retain their independent 24-entry ceiling and use the smaller of this requested limit and that ceiling. This is a wire and frame bound rather than a choice of what matters.

SlotIndex.description: One slot of the player's own inventory window, numbered as the game numbers it: 0 is the crafting result, 1 to 4 the crafting grid, 5 to 8 the armour slots, 9 to 35 the main inventory, 36 to 44 the hotbar, and 45 the off hand. Reported and named by index rather than by role, because an index is what the client library and the server both address a slot by, and because a role is a meaning - which belongs above this wire with every other meaning.

StackCount.description: How many items stand in one slot. At least one, because an empty slot is left out of the answer rather than reported as a stack of nothing - a slot reported as holding zero would tell a mind it is carrying food it does not have. The maximum is one byte's worth rather than vanilla's own stack limit of 64: a server that over-stacks a slot is reported rather than refused, because refusing the frame would blind the body over a count it read correctly, and a byte is still small enough for the largest-legal-frame arithmetic.

RetreatDistance.description: How far from a named threat a flee request asks the body to get, in blocks, as the caller states it. On the request and not a constant of the body for the same reason a sense radius is: how far away is far enough is a judgement about danger, and a body holding its own copy of it would be a second policy able to drift from the coordinator's. The maximum is the same 32 the destination of a moveTo is bounded to below, because a retreat is a walk with the goal inverted and nothing about running away may buy a body a wider reach than walking does.

MoveTolerance.description: How near the named destination counts as having arrived, in blocks, as the caller states it. Zero asks for the destination block itself. It is the caller's because it is the shape of the goal rather than a bound on the body's effort: a controller walking a body to a doorway and one walking it onto one exact block are asking for different things, and a body that supplied its own number would be choosing between them. The maximum is half the destination bound, so a tolerance can never be so wide that every reachable block satisfies it and the request answers 'arrived' without the body having moved.

MoveDeadline.description: How long the body may spend on one movement request before the request is ended as timedOut, in milliseconds, as the caller states it. Required rather than defaulted, for the reason a sense radius is: a default is the kind of number that quietly becomes the real one. The maximum is below the body process's own control-connection idle window, and that relation is the load-bearing part rather than the number: a movement is answered on the connection that asked for it, and nothing flows on that connection while the body walks, so a deadline at or above the idle window would let the socket's own timer close the channel before the answer could be written - the controller would then see a dropped connection where the contract promises exactly one answer per request. Each runtime states its own copy of both numbers and pins the ordering, because nothing on this wire is schema-validated at runtime.

EntityIndex.description: One entity of a named sense answer's own list, by its position in it, counting from zero. An index rather than a handle because a sense answer deliberately carries no handle, and rather than a position or a kind because a position is not an identity and a kind is not one either - two zombies at one distance are two threats, and a flight names one of them. The maximum is one below SenseLimit's own maximum, so every index this schema admits could name an entity of some legal answer; an index past the end of the answer actually named is refused with threatUnnamed rather than by shape, which is the same division of labour a slot index and slotUnnamed already have.

BlockIndex.description: One block of a named sense answer's own blocks list, by zero-based position. An index past the actual list is blockUnnamed rather than a malformed frame.

ItemIndex.description: One dropped item of a named sense answer's own items list, by zero-based position. An index past the actual list is itemUnnamed rather than a malformed frame.

RecipeIndex.description: One recipe of a named sense answer's own bounded recipe list, by zero-based position. An index past the actual list is recipeUnnamed rather than a malformed frame.

CraftCount.description: How many applications of one explicitly offered recipe the controller requests. The result count may be larger because one application can yield several items.

AttackCount.description: How many discrete attacks this one request may emit before it must answer. This is a strike budget, never a loop-until-death instruction.

CraftedItemCount.description: The total number of result items confirmed for one bounded craft request. Eight recipe applications yielding a full stack each is the largest legal result.

CombatHealthFloor.description: The inclusive health floor supplied by Loom for one combat request. The body stops before another attack when its latest health is at or below this value.

PursuitDistance.description: The maximum distance from the admitted position that a combat request may travel during its one optional approach. It does not permit a second search or following a moving target.

ActionDeadline.description: How long one native world interaction may remain active, in milliseconds. Required on every interaction request, positive, and below the control socket idle window so the correlated terminal answer can still be written.

BlockFace.description: The face of a sensed support block against which one held block is placed.

EquipmentDestination.description: One bounded Mineflayer player equipment destination selected by the controller.

TravelDistance.description: A distance in blocks the body itself measured, as a real number and never negative. Distances are otherwise absent from this wire on purpose - WorldPosition says so, and a sense answer reports positions and leaves every measurement to the coordinator - and the two fields carried in these units are the exceptions the rule allows rather than a softening of it. Each is a number only the body was ever in a position to take: how far it walked is summed as it walked and is the very number a travelled-distance bound was applied to, so a controller re-deriving it from two positions would be computing a second figure able to disagree with the bound that was actually enforced; and how far it ended up from a threat had to be measured while the threat was still there to measure against, which a controller reading the answer afterwards cannot do. The generation-2 maximum is one shared ceiling derived as ceil(sqrt(3 * (2 * 30000000)^2) + 128): the full diagonal between two accepted WorldPosition values plus the final bounded accumulated movement sample. It therefore carries every truthful travelled, separation and separation-change value those positions can produce, including a terminal sample taken just after the 128-block travel allowance was reached.

SeparationChange.description: How much further from a named threat the body ended up than it began, in blocks, as a signed real number. Signed because the sign is the whole of what a run needs to read from it: a flight that covered ground is not the same as a flight that gained any, and a threat that closed faster than the body ran gives a negative figure that a magnitude alone would report as success. It is the only signed number on this wire, and it is one because the two readings it is the difference of were both taken by the body - see TravelDistance. Bounded symmetrically at TravelDistance's derived generation-2 maximum so every pair of accepted positions has a truthful representation under the same one distance domain.

SensedVitals.description: The three vitals the game keeps for a player, reported as the game's own numbers and never combined into one. Health is damage to the body; food is how full the agent is; saturation is the hidden reserve that is spent before food falls. A body can be beaten to death on a full stomach and can starve without a scratch, so a wire that reported one figure for 'condition' could not say what ended an agent. The coordinator passes these same food and saturation readings into the perception contract.

health.description: Hit points, as the server last reported them. Zero is a dead player, which the lifecycle state says too. The maximum is the game's own ceiling on a max-health attribute rather than vanilla's twenty, so a server that raises it is reported rather than refused.

food.description: The food level, 0 to 20, as vanilla counts it. An integer because vanilla's food level is one, and separate from saturation because they fall in that order.

saturation.description: The hidden reserve, 0 to 20, as vanilla counts it. Never above the food level, because vanilla clamps it there when eating and spends it before food falls: a report above it has read the two at different instants. Draft 2020-12 cannot compare one property with another, so that relation is enforced by both codecs and asserted by the conformance suites, exactly as StatusReport's stateMs relation is.

SensedTime.description: The world clock, as the client library reports it and with nothing derived from it. The coordinator's own clock turns this into a phase and a countdown; a body that named the phase would be deciding what part of a day an agent is in, which is a judgement and belongs above this wire.

timeOfDay.description: Ticks since the start of the current day, 0 to 23999.

day.description: How many whole days the world has run.

isDay.description: Whether it is daylight, as the client library answers it. Reported rather than left to be derived, because it is a reading and not a calculation: a dimension whose time is fixed has a time of day and no daylight, and an agent needs the difference.

SensedGround.description: The two blocks a walking body's own footing is made of: the one it stands in and the one it stands on. Two blocks and no more - this is not a map, and a body that reported the blocks around it would be building a second world model on a wire whose frame bound could not hold one.

standingIn.description: The block at the body's own feet. Air is reported as the block it is, since air is a block the registry names.

standingOn.description: The block immediately below the body's feet.

SensedEntity.description: One entity the client library was tracking within the request's radius. It carries what the game calls it, where it is, and whether a straight line from the body's eyes reaches it - and deliberately nothing else. There is no handle: a handle that outlived the request is exactly the reuse the perception contract's own entity references refuse, and the coordinator mints one per perception from this list as it already does for its other body. There is no kind, no hostility and no threat: what an entity means is the coordinator's judgement, and a body that answered it would be deciding.

what.description: The entity kind as the game's own data names it.

visible.description: Whether a ray cast from the body's eyes to the entity reached it without meeting a block. A line and not a field of view: the body's facing is never consulted, so everything inside the radius is equally known and false here means the body knows something is there and cannot see it.

SensedBlock.description: One non-air block in the body's bounded native interaction reach. The body reports the game's name, exact block position, and current line-of-sight reading; its private sense memory retains the state needed to reject a changed block later.

position.description: The block's integer x, y, z coordinates.

visible.description: Whether Mineflayer's world ray reaches the block now. A later dig or placement revalidates this immediately before acting.

SensedItem.description: One dropped-item entity in the requested radius. The public fields identify what the game reports; the body privately retains the exact Mineflayer entity object so an entity id reused later cannot spend this offer.

visible.description: Whether a ray from the body's eyes reaches this dropped item without meeting a block.

SensedStack.description: One occupied slot of the player's own inventory window. Empty slots are left out, which is what makes the count on a reported stack at least one, and every occupied slot is reported: there is no bound to omit against and so no omission count beside the list, because a body that trimmed its own inventory would be hiding the last food an agent has.

what.description: The item as the game's own data names it, which is the same vocabulary an entity kind is reported in. Never a display name: a renamed loaf is still bread, and a display name is whatever an anvil or a datapack last called it.

SensedRecipe.description: One recipe the body could apply now from this exact inventory snapshot and, when required, one privately retained reachable crafting table. The wire reports only its result and bounded capacity; the retained recipe object, ingredient fingerprint, and workstation identity never leave the body.

resultCount.description: How many result items one application produces.

EatOutcome.description: What became of one eat request, as one value from a closed set. It is on the response rather than in ErrorCode because those are answers to different questions: an ErrorCode is why a frame was not usable, while these are what the body did about a request it understood perfectly. A refusal here is therefore an answer, and it is a value rather than prose so that a run can count how many meals were missed and why. Every refusal that is a fact about the request is settled before anything is consumed, so a refused eat never costs an agent its food. 'slotEmpty' and 'slotChanged' are kept apart because they are different facts about the run: the slot the mind named holds nothing now, against it holds something that is not what the mind chose. 'notEdible' and 'reserveFull' are kept apart for the same reason and it is the sharper of the two pairs: an agent that had nothing edible to eat and an agent that ate itself to a standstill and could not use the rest are opposite readings of the same run, and vanilla itself refuses the second - a full food bar cannot take an ordinary food, whatever the agent is carrying. 'slotInaccessible' is the residual, and the one outcome that cannot promise the food is still there: the stack was there and was edible and the meal still did not happen, because the body could not bring it to hand or the game never confirmed it - and a use the game never confirmed may still have been carried out, which is exactly why it reads as a fault to go and look at rather than as a fact about the agent.

MoveOutcome.description: What became of one movement request, as one value from a closed set, and shared by a walk and a flight because both are one route to one goal and a run counting either wants the same words. It is on the response and not in ErrorCode for the reason an EatOutcome is: an ErrorCode says a frame was not usable, and these say what the body did about a request it understood. Every value is either an arrival, a bound that ended the request, or a fact about a named threat, and the three groups are kept apart in the order below rather than collapsed, because a run that could not tell them apart could not say whether its bodies were blocked, throttled or chasing threats that were never there. 'noRoute' is the ground's own answer - the library searched every node it was allowed to and found nothing - while 'stalled' is a route that was found and then abandoned, which is a different thing to go and look at. 'searchOverBudget' is neither, and it is the one outcome on this list that is a fact about the body process rather than about the world: the body's own search budget stopped a search that had not finished, so nothing at all is known about the ground. It is separate from 'noRoute' because collapsing the two is a lie in the direction that matters - a controller told the ground refused a route, when the truth is that the body would not spend any longer looking, and for a flee that reads as nowhere to run. A controller that meets it may ask again, closer or with the same target, and may reasonably treat a repeat as the body being too busy to search rather than as the world being closed. 'overTravelled' and 'timedOut' are the two bounds a request can walk into after a route was found, and they are separate because distance and duration fail for unrelated reasons: a body pacing a short loop runs out of blocks, and a body waiting on a slow search runs out of time. 'cancelled' is the answer to a halt or to the connection going away, and it is an outcome rather than a refusal because the request was carried out up to the moment it was stopped and its measurements are worth reporting. 'outOfRange' is refused before anything is searched for, so its travelled field is exactly zero; both codecs enforce that relation and the beyond-schema corpus pins the nonzero form because this schema deliberately keeps all field relations in one runtime mechanism. The last three are reachable only by a flee, because only a flee names a threat: 'senseForgotten' and 'threatUnnamed' are the handle refusals a slot handle already has by those names, and 'threatGone' is an entity the body could not find - whether it never resolved or vanished while the body ran from it, which are the same fact about a flight that has nothing left to measure separation against.

DigOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to one dig. The first is a vanilla-confirmed block break; the next seven are exact pre-application facts; timedOut and cancelled stop an active dig; libraryFailure is the bounded residual when Mineflayer could not confirm a more specific result.

CollectOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to collecting one exact dropped-item entity. Movement endings retain the same spelling and meaning as MoveOutcome; collected is emitted only for Mineflayer's pickup event naming this body and this exact retained entity object.

PlaceOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to one placement against one sensed support block with one offered stack that was already held. placed is Mineflayer's confirmed block update; every other value either names the exact revalidation that refused the packet or states that the bounded library operation ended without such confirmation.

EquipOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to equipping one offered stack into one chosen equipment destination. equipped is reported only after the client inventory shows that exact stack at Mineflayer's actual destination slot.

CraftOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to one bounded craft. crafted is emitted only after the requested applications complete and the result inventory delta is confirmed; the remaining values distinguish request authority, live ingredients, workstation state, bounds, lifecycle endings, and the library residual.

AttackOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to attacking one exact retained living entity with one exact retained inventory stack. attacked means the requested strike budget was emitted while the target remained live; targetDied means the exact target died first. Movement outcomes describe only the one optional fixed-position approach.

SayText.description: One line of player chat the controller chose verbatim. Nothing is normalised: the accepted text is the exact text sent. At most 128 code points, and both codecs also refuse more than 256 UTF-8 bytes or any unpaired surrogate, which JSON Schema cannot state. Words are separated by exactly one U+0020 and the line may not begin or end with whitespace, because vanilla normalises chat whitespace and the server-observed text must equal the sent text. It may not begin with '/', which Mineflayer would send as a command. C0/C1 controls, DEL, the section-sign formatting escape, other Unicode spaces, zero-width and bidirectional controls, line separators, the BOM and interlinear annotation characters are refused.

SayOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to one say. sent means Mineflayer's player chat primitive wrote exactly one chat packet with the exact text; it is a client acknowledgement and not proof the server attributed the message. rateLimited means the body's bounded per-agent window was full and nothing was sent.

SleepOutcome.description: Every terminal answer to one sleep at one exact retained bed. woke means vanilla accepted the sleep and later woke this body; a timeout or cancellation may occur either before or after entry and the report states that separately.

LifecycleState.description: Where the body process is in its one life. Seven states and no gameplay: this says whether there is a player on the server and whether it is still usable, never what the player should do. 'connecting' is before the server has accepted the login; 'loggedIn' is after the login packet and before the first spawn; 'ready' is a spawned, live player; 'dead' is a player the server has killed, which the process reports and never respawns; 'disconnected' is a connection the server or the network ended; 'stopping' is a shutdown in progress; 'failed' is a client error the process could not continue from. 'loggedIn' and 'dead' are separate from 'ready' for a reason found in world: a dead identity reconnecting arrives on the death screen, so it reaches loggedIn and then dead without ever reaching ready.

ControlOperation.description: What a controller may ask for. The operation set is the one part of a generation that may grow without moving the generation: an older body refuses an operation it does not know as unknownOperation, while a body-chosen response field or enum value can surprise a controller after an operation it did know and therefore requires a new generation. Generation 4 added craft, attack, and sleep, but moved because sense and response value sets widened, not merely because those request names existed. Generation 5 widens only the body-chosen world-observation lists. say was added within generation 5: its closed outcome set answers only a controller that sent say, so no agreed frame widened.

ErrorCode.description: Why a request was refused, as one value from a closed set. It is an enum and not a message on purpose, and this is the one place the body-control protocol is deliberately stricter than the cognition wire's free-text refusal: an exception string, a file path, a host name or a token cannot reach a controller or a log through a field that can only hold one of these words. A controller that needs more than the code has the code to search for.

BodyRequest.description: One request from a controller to a body process. Internally tagged on the 'op' property. Every variant carries the protocol generation, the correlation id its one answer will echo, and the agent whose body is being addressed - so a frame is self-describing and a reply can never be matched to the wrong request. Four lifecycle or cancellation variants carry no payload at all. Every action payload carries only the controller's own bounds and exact choices from a retained sense answer - a slot, place, creature, recipe, weapon, or bed - and never a body-owned threshold or selection rule. A named place is the opposite of body policy: a destination a controller states is the controller having decided, and a body given one searches for a route to it and reports what it found. What would make the body a decider is a target it chose itself - the nearest food, somewhere safe, a recipe to make, a creature to hunt, a bed to use - and no operation here admits one.

oneOf.title: Handshake
oneOf.description: Agree the protocol generation and learn who the process is. It must be the first request on a connection: any other operation before it is refused with handshakeRequired, so a controller cannot read a field this generation happens to share with the next. Repeating it on the same connection is allowed and answered the same way, because a handshake reports state rather than changing it.

oneOf.title: Status
oneOf.description: Ask what state the body is in. This is also the protocol's correlated ping: an answer echoing the requestId is itself the proof that the process is alive and reading its socket, so there is no separate ping operation to keep in step with it.

oneOf.title: Shutdown
oneOf.description: Stop the body process. It is answered before anything is closed, so a controller learns the shutdown was accepted rather than inferring it from a dropped socket. Repeating it is answered the same way rather than refused: a controller that did not see the first answer must be able to ask again without having to know whether it arrived.

oneOf.title: Sense
oneOf.description: Read the raw state the game reports about the player: its vitals, the world clock, its footing, the entities, blocks, dropped items, and craftable recipes the client library can currently offer, and every occupied slot of its inventory. The two bounds are the caller's own and are required rather than defaulted, because a body that supplied a default would own a perception policy it has no business owning - and a default is the kind of number that quietly becomes the real one. Answered only for a spawned, live player whose readings the game has actually reported: any other lifecycle state is refused with notReady, since a body that has not spawned has no position to read and one that has been removed would be reporting the world it last saw - and so is a spawned player the server has not yet told the time of day, or whose vitals do not yet make sense together, because a reading the body would have to invent to fill a required field is not a reading.

oneOf.title: Eat
oneOf.description: Eat the one stack standing in the slot a named sense reported. It names a slot of one earlier answer rather than a food, so two stacks of bread are two different meals and one of them may be the last food the agent has - and the body chooses nothing: it has no threshold, no timer, no target selection and no notion of which food is better. The senseId is the requestId of the sense whose answer the choice was made from, which is what makes the reference request-scoped: the body remembers only its most recent few answers, so a slot named from an older one is refused with senseForgotten rather than looked up in the inventory as it stands now. Answered only for a spawned, live player whose readings the game has reported, for the reason a sense is: the vitals ride every eat answer, refusal included, so a body that cannot state them cannot answer an eat either.

senseId.description: The requestId of the sense answer the slot was chosen from. A ControlId because that is what it is - one echoed back - and not a new kind of handle.

oneOf.title: MoveTo
oneOf.description: Walk to one place the controller names, and answer once when the walk has ended. The destination is absolute world coordinates rather than an offset, because an offset would have to be applied to a position the body read for itself and a controller would then be naming somewhere it had never seen. Bounded twice over: a destination further from the body than 32 blocks when the request arrives is refused with outOfRange before any search is run, and the body carries its own ceilings on search time, per-tick search time, retries and distance walked - those are the body's because they are costs to the process rather than judgements about the world, and a controller able to raise them could stall the process from outside. Only one movement runs at a time: a moveTo or a flee arriving while either is still running is refused with notReady rather than taking the route over, so a controller can never silently displace a request it has not seen the answer to. Answered only for a spawned, live player, for the reason a sense is - a body that has not spawned has no position to walk from. The answer comes when the route ends and not when it is accepted, so a controller holds one request open for the whole walk; the deadline it states is what bounds that wait.

destination.description: Where the body is being sent, in absolute world coordinates. Refused with outOfRange, without searching, if it is more than 32 blocks from where the body stands when the request arrives.

sprint.description: Whether the body may sprint on this route. False is not a performance setting: sprinting spends food, so a body allowed to sprint whenever it could would be quietly deciding to be hungrier, which is a survival decision and the controller's. True is the controller saying it accepts that cost for this one request.

oneOf.title: Flee
oneOf.description: Run from one creature a named sense reported, and answer once when the flight has ended. It names an entity of one earlier answer by that answer's own ordering rather than by kind or by position, for the reason an eat names a slot rather than a food: two zombies at one distance are two threats and a flight is from one of them, a kind is not an identity, and a position is a place the threat has already left. That makes the reference request-scoped exactly as a slot reference is - the body remembers only its most recent few sense answers, so a threat named from an older one is refused with senseForgotten, and an index past the end of the answer that was named is refused with threatUnnamed. The goal is a fixed snapshot of where the threat stood when the flight began, and deliberately not a goal that follows it: one request gets one answer here, and a goal that moved would be the body re-deciding where to go for as long as the request lasted. Every bound a moveTo is under applies unchanged - the same reach, the same body-side ceilings, the same one-movement-at-a-time refusal - because running away may not buy a body anything walking does not have.

senseId.description: The requestId of the sense answer the threat was chosen from. A ControlId for the reason an eat's is - one echoed back, and not a new kind of handle.

sprint.description: Whether the body may sprint away. Spelled and meant exactly as a moveTo's is, and not defaulted to true for a flight: whether outrunning this threat is worth the food is the judgement the coordinator is there to make, and a body that assumed it would be deciding on the controller's behalf in the one situation where the cost matters most.

oneOf.title: Halt
oneOf.description: Stop whichever cancellable movement or world interaction is running. It carries no payload because there is at most one conflicting owner. The stopped request receives its own cancelled terminal outcome; this request separately reports whether anything was stopped.

oneOf.title: Dig
oneOf.description: Dig one block offered by one retained sense answer, using only the item already held. The body revalidates identity, state, visibility, reach, and diggability immediately before invoking Mineflayer.

oneOf.title: Collect
oneOf.description: Collect one exact dropped-item entity offered by one retained sense answer. approach explicitly permits one bounded path to the entity's admitted position; false permits no movement. The body never follows a moving target or chooses a substitute.

oneOf.title: Place
oneOf.description: Place one offered stack that is already in the selected main hand against one chosen face of one offered support block. The support, destination, held stack, visibility, and reach are revalidated immediately before the single Mineflayer placement.

oneOf.title: Equip
oneOf.description: Equip one stack offered by one retained sense answer into one chosen bounded destination. The exact slot contents are re-read before Mineflayer is invoked; Mineflayer's actual destination slot is reported.

oneOf.title: Craft
oneOf.description: Apply one recipe offered by one retained sense answer a bounded number of times. The offer privately retains the exact recipe, full ingredient snapshot, and any required crafting table. All three are revalidated before the first inventory transaction; no ingredient is gathered and no substitute recipe or table is chosen.

oneOf.title: Attack
oneOf.description: Attack one exact living entity and use one exact offered inventory stack for at most the stated number of strikes. approach permits one route to the target's admitted position, never a pursuit loop; maxPursuitDistance bounds that route and later target displacement. The body revalidates target identity, target life, weapon stack, health floor, and range before every strike.

oneOf.title: Say
oneOf.description: Send one bounded line through this agent's own Mineflayer player chat, never a server console broadcast. One-shot: the body sends at most one chat packet, chooses no text, and starts no follow-on action or reply.

oneOf.title: Sleep
oneOf.description: Sleep in one exact bed offered by one retained sense answer and hold the request until vanilla wakes the body or a bound ends it. No time-of-day policy or night-skip decision lives here: Mineflayer asks the server to use this bed once and reports the server's result.

BodyResponse.description: The answer to one request the process understood. Internally tagged on the same 'op' the request named, and carrying that request's own requestId and agentId back, so a controller matches an answer by id rather than by arrival order. Exactly one BodyResponse or one BodyError is written per request.

oneOf.title: HandshakeAccepted
oneOf.description: The protocol generation is agreed and the process names itself. The username is the identity a controller would see on the server's own player list, which is what lets an operator tie a control channel to a player without the process reporting anything about the world.

oneOf.title: StatusReport
oneOf.description: Where the body is in its life, and how long it has been there. Both durations are milliseconds measured by the process's own monotonic clock rather than a wall clock, so neither goes backwards when the host's time is adjusted. Still deliberately no position, health, hunger, inventory, or world offers, now that a sense answer carries them: a status report is what a controller asks for on a schedule to learn whether the process is alive, and a liveness check that dragged the world along with it would make every such poll cost a full read and would give two frames the same answer to keep in step. The bounded answer to 'what does the game say about this player' is SenseReport below, and it is asked for by name.

uptimeMs.description: How long the process has been running.

stateMs.description: How long the process has been in the state it reports. Never larger than uptimeMs, since a process starts in a state. Draft 2020-12 cannot compare one property with another, so that relation is enforced by both codecs and asserted semantically by the conformance suites rather than by this schema - which is why it is stated here as a rule and not merely as prose.

requestsHandled.description: How many requests the process has answered, refusals included, counting this one. At least one, because answering this status request is itself handling a request: a report of zero has miscounted its own answer. A controller comparing it with its own count learns whether anything was lost without the process having to log a request.

oneOf.title: ShutdownAccepted
oneOf.description: The shutdown was accepted and is under way. The state is always 'stopping': it is the one terminal state the protocol reports, and it is written before the Minecraft connection or the control channel is closed.

oneOf.title: SenseReport
oneOf.description: What the game says about this player, at one instant and with nothing derived from it. Every reading in one answer is taken together, so a distance the coordinator computes between two of them is one reading of a moving world rather than two that can disagree. The state is always 'ready', since no other state can be sensed. Nothing here is measured, sorted into kinds, or judged: the coordinator turns positions into distances, bearings and heights, decides what is a threat, mints the handles a mind may name, and applies its own further bounds. What the body does do is cut the entity list to the limit it was given, nearest first, and say how many it dropped - because the cut has to be made where the distances were measured, and an answer that reported the cut without the count would read afterwards as a quiet scene, which is the one reading a survival run must never be given.

position.description: Where the body itself is standing. First among the readings because every other position in the answer is only meaningful beside it.

ground.description: The body's own footing, when the body could read it. Absent means the client library had no block there to report, which happens when the chunk the body is standing in has not arrived yet - and absent must never be read as air, because an unread chunk reporting air is how a body comes to believe it is standing over a hole it never looked at. Present or absent is therefore a fact about what was read, not about what is there.

entities.description: The entities the client library was tracking within the radius, nearest first, cut to the limit the request named. Nearest first because that is the order a cut has to be made in for the survivors to be the ones worth keeping, and because a caller applying a tighter bound of its own can then take a prefix. Neither codec checks the order, and that is deliberate rather than an omission: the body sorts by the distance from its eyes, which is not the position this list carries, so a check at either end would be a second and disagreeing measurement of the same scene. It is pinned where it is decided, in the body's own tests.

entitiesOmitted.description: How many entities were inside the radius and did not fit the limit. Zero when nothing was dropped. It rides inside the answer rather than being left for a caller to work out, because the caller cannot: the number the body cut against is the only place the dropped ones were ever counted, and a caller adding its own cut to this one counts each bound exactly once.

blocks.description: Nearby non-air blocks inside the body's fixed native interaction reach, nearest first, cut independently to the request limit.

blocksOmitted.description: How many otherwise describable blocks inside native interaction reach did not fit the request limit.

items.description: Dropped-item entities inside the request radius, nearest first, cut independently to the request limit.

itemsOmitted.description: How many otherwise describable dropped-item entities inside the radius did not fit the request limit.

inventory.description: Every occupied slot of the player's own inventory window, in slot order. Complete rather than bounded: the window has 46 slots and all of them may be reported, so there is no omission count here and no way for the body to have hidden a stack. A slot that is empty is left out, which is why a reported stack always holds at least one item. Slot order is strictly increasing, and both codecs enforce it, which no keyword here can say. That makes it two rules in one: the order a reader may rely on, and the statement that no slot is described twice - a repeated slot is a body that read its own window wrongly, and an eat naming it would resolve against whichever of the two descriptions happened to be found first.

recipes.description: Recipes that can be applied from this exact inventory and any privately retained reachable crafting table, ordered deterministically by result and recipe fingerprint and cut to the request limit.

recipesOmitted.description: How many otherwise offerable recipes did not fit the request limit.

oneOf.title: EatReport
oneOf.description: What became of one eat request. The outcome carries the whole of the answer, and the vitals are always reported beside it - including on a refusal, because a controller that asked to eat is deciding what to do next from how full the agent is, and a refusal that said nothing about that would send it back for a second read. 'state' and 'vitals' are both the moment the request was admitted rather than the moment the frame was written, and this is the one operation where those differ: a meal is answered after two round trips to the server, so the body can die, disconnect or be handed a food level outside vanilla's own ceiling in between. The 'ready' this frame states is therefore not a claim about now but about the moment the numbers beside it came from, and a writer prefers a fresher vitals reading only while the body is still in that state and the reading can still be stated, carrying the admitted reading whole otherwise, never a mix of the two. 'what' and 'remaining' are present exactly when the outcome is 'eaten': they say which item was consumed and how many of it the body still held when it last looked, which is what a run counts consumption from, and a refusal has consumed nothing to describe. Exactly one item is consumed, by the client library's own use of the item rather than by arithmetic here.

what.description: The item that was eaten, as the game's own data names it. Present exactly when the outcome is 'eaten'.

remaining.description: How many of that item the body still holds, counted where the stack ended up after the body brought it to hand rather than in the slot the request named: bringing a stack to hand moves it, so the named slot is not where the meal came from by the time one is eaten, and a count read there would be a count of whatever the move left behind. Zero when the last one was eaten. It is the body's latest observation rather than a promised delta on the count the sense answer offered: the server states a consumed slot in a packet of its own, the body waits a bounded moment for it, and past that bound it reports the count as it stands rather than refusing a meal that has already happened. Exactly one item was consumed either way. Present exactly when the outcome is 'eaten'. Draft 2020-12 could express that relation as a conditional, and deliberately does not: the two codecs enforce it and the conformance suites assert it, as they do for every other relation this schema states in prose.

oneOf.title: MoveReport
oneOf.description: What became of one moveTo. The outcome carries the whole of the answer and the four readings beside it are always present, refusals included: a request refused before anything was searched for has walked nowhere, which is a measurement of zero rather than an absence, and a controller that asked a body to walk needs to know where the body is whatever the answer was. 'state' is the moment the request was admitted rather than the moment the frame was written, for the reason an EatReport's is and more sharply: a walk is answered when the route ends, so seconds pass in between and the body can die or disconnect inside them. The 'ready' this frame states is therefore about the moment the walk began. Three of the eleven MoveOutcome values are unreachable here, because a walk names no threat: 'senseForgotten', 'threatUnnamed' and 'threatGone' can only answer a flee. Draft 2020-12 could express that with an enum narrowed for this variant, and deliberately does not, for the reason every other relation in this file is left to the codecs: one MoveOutcome shared by both reports is what makes a run able to count arrivals and bounds across walks and flights without translating between two enums, and both codecs refuse a walk that names a threat refusal.

from.description: Where the body stood when the request was admitted. Reported rather than left for a controller to remember, because the controller may not have sensed at that instant and a displacement measured against a position from some earlier moment is a displacement of the wrong walk.

position.description: Where the body stood when the request ended. This and 'from' are the whole of the displacement, and no straight-line figure is derived from them here: two positions the coordinator can subtract are exactly what a sense answer already gives it, and a body computing the difference as well would be a second measurement able to disagree with the one the coordinator takes.

travelled.description: How far the body actually walked, summed as it walked. Not the straight line between the two positions and not derivable from them: a body that went round a wall covered more ground than the line says, and a body that walked a loop covered a great deal while the line says nothing at all. It is on the wire because it is the very number the body's own distance ceiling was applied to, so a controller re-deriving it would be checking a bound against a figure that is not the one enforced - which is the same reason a sense answer carries its own omission count.

elapsedMs.description: How long the request took, from admission to this answer, by the process's own monotonic clock. It is what the deadline was measured against, so a 'timedOut' outcome states the bound it hit rather than leaving a reader to infer it, and an 'arrived' states what the walk cost.

oneOf.title: FleeReport
oneOf.description: What became of one flee. Every field a MoveReport carries means the same thing here and is spelled the same way, because a flight is a walk with an inverted goal and a run counting displacement should not have to read two vocabularies. Two fields are added, and both are measurements only the body could take: how far from the threat it ended up, and how much of that it gained. They are present exactly when the outcome is not one of the three threat refusals - 'senseForgotten', 'threatUnnamed' and 'threatGone' - because each of those three is the body saying it had no threat to measure against: the first two never resolved one, and the third had one that was gone by the time the flight ended. Draft 2020-12 could express that relation as a conditional and deliberately does not, exactly as EatReport's own conditional presence is left to the codecs and the conformance suites. Note that a flight ending because the threat vanished is not a failure and is not reported as one: the body did what it was asked and there is simply nothing left to state a separation about.

from.description: Where the body stood when the request was admitted. Spelled and meant exactly as a MoveReport's is.

position.description: Where the body stood when the request ended. Spelled and meant exactly as a MoveReport's is.

travelled.description: How far the body actually walked. Spelled and meant exactly as a MoveReport's is, and it is the field that must not be read as progress: ground covered is not ground gained, which is what 'separationGained' is for.

elapsedMs.description: How long the request took. Spelled and meant exactly as a MoveReport's is.

separation.description: How far the body ended up from the threat, measured against where the threat actually was at that moment rather than against the snapshot the goal was built from. The live reading is the honest one: a threat that chased the body is nearer than the snapshot says, and that is the fact a coordinator has to act on. Present exactly when the outcome is not a threat refusal.

separationGained.description: How much further from the threat the body ended up than it began - this answer's own separation less the same measurement taken when the request was admitted. Signed, and the sign is the point: a negative figure is a threat that closed faster than the body ran, which is a flight that failed while covering plenty of ground, and it is the one thing a magnitude alone could not say. Present exactly when the outcome is not a threat refusal, for the same reason 'separation' is.

oneOf.title: DigReport
oneOf.description: What became of one dig. attempted distinguishes a pre-application refusal from an operation handed to Mineflayer; tool is the actual main-hand item Mineflayer used and is absent for bare hand or when nothing was attempted. dug is this body's own break: the server's update answered its own finish. blockGone is either a block found gone before the dig was handed to Mineflayer, or one another player broke while this body was still digging it, which is attempted.

tool.description: The item actually held when Mineflayer started the dig. Absent for bare hand and for a request refused before Mineflayer was invoked.

oneOf.title: CollectReport
oneOf.description: What became of collecting one exact dropped-item entity, including the bounded journey. what and count are present exactly when the matching Mineflayer pickup event confirmed this body collected the retained entity object.

oneOf.title: PlaceReport
oneOf.description: What became of one placement. what, position, and remaining are present exactly when Mineflayer observed the destination change and confirmed one block was placed.

oneOf.title: EquipReport
oneOf.description: What became of one equip. what, count, and toSlot are present exactly when the client inventory confirms the offered stack at Mineflayer's actual destination slot; toSlot records Mineflayer's hand-slot choice separately from the controller's destination.

oneOf.title: CraftReport
oneOf.description: What became of one craft. attempted says whether at least one bounded recipe application was handed to Mineflayer; it can be false for a timeout or cancellation before the first application and true for a later revalidation failure after an earlier application. what, count, and crafts are present exactly when the full requested result was confirmed.

oneOf.title: AttackReport
oneOf.description: What became of one bounded combat request. The journey records the one optional approach and attacks is the exact number of attack packets emitted for this request, including when a later bound or target death ended it.

oneOf.title: SleepReport
oneOf.description: What became of one sleep request. entered says whether the exact body was observed sleeping before the terminal outcome, so a timeout after entering cannot be mistaken for a refusal that had no vanilla effect.

oneOf.title: SayReport
oneOf.description: What became of one say. It echoes no text: the controller holds what it asked for, and the server's own chat event is the attribution evidence.

oneOf.title: HaltReport
oneOf.description: What one halt did. stopped false means no cancellable movement or interaction was active; stopped true means the owning request is also answered with its own cancelled outcome.

stopped.description: Whether a movement was in fact running and has been stopped.

BodyError.description: A refusal. It is not a BodyResponse and carries no 'op', because a frame the process could not decode has no operation to name - the same reasoning that keeps the cognition wire's refusal frame outside the perception/decision contract. The agentId is always present, since the process knows its own identity whatever arrived on the socket; the requestId is present only when the frame carried a readable one, because echoing an id the process never received would put a fiction on the wire and let a controller match a refusal to a request that does not exist.
